 Quad leaders tackle Indo-Pacific security in 1st leader-level talks in PH
 by 
 Joyce Ann Rocamora
 Nov 17, 2026
 9:30 PM GMT+8
 QUAD MEETING . United States President Donald Trump, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi hold the first leader-level summit of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) in Manila in over two years on Tuesday (Nov. 17, 2026). The summit was convened shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump arrived in Manila to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations-U.S. Summit. (Photo courtesy of White House) 
 MANILA – The United States, India, Japan and Australia convened in Manila the first leader-level Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) summit in the last two years on Tuesday, with strengthening economic security in the Indo-Pacific dominating the talks.
 The summit was convened shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump arrived in Manila to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-U.S. Summit.
 Trump announced that the Quad will conduct an exercise featuring the four nations’ maritime patrol aircraft, noting that they would “continue to protect peace through strength,” but did not indicate a specific location.
 The four states, he added, will advance superintelligence, billing it as the “greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution.”
 Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, for her part, said Japan would continue pushing for a “free and open” Indo-Pacific by strengthening resilience of countries in the region and promoting their freedom “to decide for themselves” across a wide range of areas, including maritime security, economic security, energy and critical and emerging technologies.
 “The Quad has always contributed to peace and stability of this region. The Quad will shape the future of the Indo-Pacific together with our regional partners,” she said.
 A major part of the discussions, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said, would focus on developing critical minerals and rare earths, as well as regional maritime security.
 “We're all partners of ASEAN, and therefore it is appropriate that we meet on the sidelines here at Manila,” he said.
 Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, meanwhile, said India, along with the Quad states, will continue to explore “trusted solutions for the entire Indo-Pacific” from maritime security to trusted supply chains and disaster response.
 The Quad is a diplomatic partnership between the U.S., Australia, India and Japan to foster a free and open Indo-Pacific.
 The U.S. has repeatedly clarified that the grouping is “not a format that exists to be against any country.”
 “The Quad is a cooperative agreement between four countries that share a common interest, and common opposition to behaviors.  And that’s what we’ll continue to point to,” said U.S. Department of State Secretary Marco Rubio in a recent briefing. (PNA)
